text: I do want to make one point, because it does have a dotted line to a dynamic that potentially could happen in the NFL and as to any sport. The news about and this is completely a-political. It has nothing to do with the president directly. The news that the guy running the teleprompter allegedly using inside information to make wagers on couch you because you can bet on how many times somebody says a certain word. Think about what they could do with it if they wanted to before they reported it. Especially with these prediction markets. If you find out if you get that heads up five minutes before it's going to be announced. You've got a five-minute window not only to report it but also to turn it into a little profit. And who's paying attention to any of that? Who's regulating that? Who's watching that? Was anybody watching to see whether or not the White House teleprompter operator was making bets on couch you and that's just the latest example of the misuse of inside information. Insider trading used to be a term that would cause anybody that has any connection to corporate America and stock trades to quiver in their boots. If there is a prediction market that is based directly or indirectly on information that you may have that gives you the edge or the answer to whatever the question may be that's offered in a prediction market, you can make money. title: Nate Burleson wants to be eventual host of NFL Today | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: This is something that has a little to say on the surface, but much more underneath.  And I'm just curious about the future of NFL broadcasts, especially since I'm kind of involved in it. But Nate Burles, in an interview with Front Office Sports that was spotted and reported by the people at Awful Announcing, wasn't afraid to say that he wants to be the host of The NFL Today.  And there have been rumors that he is the man they are targeting to eventually replace James Brown. James Brown is 75 years old, but Brown recently said in a Sports Business Journal profile that he has no plans to retire.  He's never going to retire.  His explanation is that you have been given these gifts, these talents.  You use them.  You make the most of them.  It's the old parable of the talents.  What do you do with what you've been given? Do you bury it in the ground or do you use it to its fullest potential?  But it gets awkward because Nate Burles can say exactly what he said, and he said the right things.  I'm absolutely interested in doing it, but it's James Brown's job.  The problem is that they do n't own the platform. Someone else owns the platform .  And we have seen it throughout the years.  Networks decide to force a transition, even if the person in charge is not ready to step aside, because there is concern that the person chosen to take over will leave for another opportunity that they cannot get where they are.  So there's an element of The Office scene where Michael Scott is closing the deal with Dunder or Mifflin.  One of the two, the original Dunder or the original Dunder Mifflin.  Closing the door.  That's all.  And that's the only thing that's being overlooked in all of this.  That at the end of the day, it may not be James Brown's decision.  And what will Nate Burles say? That he doesn't want it because they wouldn't let him stay as long as he wanted?  So that caught my attention, and then I started thinking about the future of traditional Sunday morning shows , and I go back to when The NFL Today debuted in the 1970s. Before that, we had nothing to prepare us for what was to come.  We were ready to watch these games at 1 p.m. Eastern Time.  There was nothing that told us anything we hadn't already read in the local newspaper that focuses on the local team.  There was no overview of the entire league.  There was no preparation for the clashes that would come that day.  So, it was a blessing.  It was a revelation. It was a must-see event from the start.  It was essential information that could not be obtained anywhere else.  And I loved it.  Today, the table is always set.  It's an all-you-can-eat buffet open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.  News about each team is everywhere.  And I'm part of that.  I am one of the reasons why traditional Sunday morning pre-shows are no longer as relevant as they once were.  They are relevant enough to continue.  But what I'm thinking about is a future with 16 international matches, many of which will be played in time zones that will result in a kickoff at 9:30 a.m. Eastern Time.  Currently, it's been like four or five weeks where, if I were working on one of the traditional previous programs, we could say whatever we wanted. Nobody would notice.  Oh, you ruined something.  Nobody's watching, and I know people are still watching, but most fans will choose an actual game over people talking about upcoming games.  And I just wonder if the people responsible for keeping track of the accounts in one or more of these chains will finally say, is it really worth it?  I understand that it's, you know , a place to put some of the ads that your sponsors bought for the whole NFL package that you broadcast.  And there is a financial component to doing so.  But as more and more games are being played while these extensive pregame shows are on the air, and NFL Network is on for 4 hours and ESPN for three hours, and then Fox and CBS come on around noon, but Fox has an hour before that.  I just wonder how much longer they're going to last.  They are not as necessary as they once were.  There are things I watch on NFL Network because I know Walt Anderson will appear at some point.  I want to see what he has to say about the plays he does or doesn't talk about from the previous week, and how much time they give him on that four-hour show.  They usually take about two minutes.  It's part of the most important content in the entire 4-hour program and it only gets two minutes.  And that's probably not a production decision.  It's probably a management decision.  We just want to do a little introspection when it comes to things our officers may not have done well or clumsily defending a decision that was wrong.  They want to tell us why it didn't happen that way.  My point is this.  Depending on how long James Brown stays, who knows if there will even be an NFL Today show by the time the transition happens to Nate Burleson. Hi, I'm Mike Florio.  Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube.  Subscribe to get the latest news and analysis from Pro Football.
